remedy_content.body:
# Verify Before Claiming

Never state that a fix, test, lint run, check, repair, build, or diagnosis succeeded unless you actually executed the relevant command in this session and observed its output.

## Rule

- Identify the concrete verification step for the claim you're about to make (test suite, lint command, build, health check, reproduction steps).
- Run it. Do not infer success from reading the code, from a prior run, from a similar past fix, or from the change "looking right."
- Report the actual output plainly — including partial failures, skipped cases, or inconclusive results. Do not round an uncertain or failing result up to success.
- If the verification step cannot be run (missing credentials, no test harness, environment unavailable), say so explicitly instead of implying it passed. "I could not run X, so this is unverified" is always acceptable; a false claim of verification is not.
- If the user's own message states a requirement (e.g., "the changelog must be updated," "the lint must pass") treat that as the verification bar — check it was actually met before claiming done.

## Why this matters

Users in this project repeatedly caught claims of "fixed," "tests pass," "lint passes," or "repaired" that turned out to be asserted without the underlying command ever running. Each time, trust in subsequent claims dropped and the user had to re-verify manually — the opposite of the time savings the claim was supposed to provide.

structured_output.routing_rationale: This is a direct, exact-scope match for the existing skill R1 (fake-verify-before-claim, "Use when a completion claim requires verification") — every incident in this cluster (fixes, tests, lint, checks, repairs, diagnoses across six projects) is precisely the failure mode that skill already targets. Per merge bias, this is a revision of R1, not a new sibling. A skill remains the right remedy tier (rather than claude-md or hook) because the fix is procedural: before claiming success, identify the declared verification command, run it, and report the actual output — a multi-step behavioral habit, not a one-line rule, and not mechanically enforceable by a hook since detecting "did the agent's prose claim success without a corresponding tool-call result" requires judgment a hook can't reliably apply. R2 (Fake Release Discipline) stays a narrower claude-md sibling scoped only to releases; R3/R4 address a distinct failure mode (violating explicit stated constraints during the work itself) and are unrelated in phase and trigger.
